Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Dr. Rafael Morales, a 40-year-old Latin American surgeon, still vividly remembers the day Hurricane Maria ravaged his hometown in Puerto Rico three years ago. As he recounts the event, his voice trembles with grief. "I was on call at the hospital when the storm hit. The howling winds and creaking walls were like nothing I'd ever experienced before." He recalls trying to secure the doors and windows, but they burst open, flooding the wards with water and debris. As Rafael navigated the chaos, a massive electrical fire broke out in one of the operating rooms. "I remember the smell of smoke and burnt flesh... it was overwhelming," he says, his eyes welling up with tears. The image of patients frantically trying to escape the burning ward haunts him still. Rafael's face contorts as he recounts how the hospital staff fought to save lives amidst the inferno. In the aftermath, Rafael began experiencing inexplicable triggers that transported him back to that fateful day. Loud noises – a car alarm or thunderstorm – would send his heart racing and palms sweating. The smell of smoke or fire would instantly bring back memories of the burning ward, making him feel helpless all over again. Even the faint scent of burnt food could evoke an intense emotional response. To cope with these visceral reactions, Rafael turned to various maladaptive strategies. He began indulging in substance use – drinking more frequently and relying on medication to calm his nerves. He'd also distract himself by binge-watching TV shows or immersing himself in video games, attempting to quiet the turmoil brewing inside. Furthermore, he started using sex as a coping mechanism – fantasizing about intimate encounters with women other than his wife. These attempts at self-soothing came at a cost. Rafael's relationship with his wife began to fray. She'd notice his distant behavior and accuse him of being detached from their marital life. As the months went by, Rafael became increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings or events that might trigger memories of the disaster. One aspect that still plagues Rafael is the fragmented nature of his memories. He recalls snatches of conversations with patients, but other moments remain shrouded in uncertainty. This feeling of an incomplete picture torments him – what did he miss? What could he have done differently? Grief on recall has become a constant companion for Rafael. When memories resurface, the overwhelming sense of despair threatens to engulf him anew. He finds himself wondering if there's still hope for healing. As a surgeon, Rafael is acutely aware of his own vulnerabilities – physical and emotional. The stress of his occupation had always been manageable, but now the pressure feels suffocating. His surgical skills are compromised by tremors and anxiety, making it increasingly difficult to perform procedures with confidence. The breaking point came when Rafael botched a routine operation due to his shaking hands. Ashamed and scared for his patients' safety, he realized that his avoidance strategies were no longer tenable. He couldn't continue living like this – constantly walking on eggshells, afraid of what memories the next trigger would unlock. Seeking help has become an admission of defeat for Rafael, but also a glimmer of hope. As he begins to unravel the tangled threads of his traumatic experience, he's starting to confront the fears that have held him captive for so long. His primary concern is whether therapy can help him regain control over his memories and emotions – or if the past will forever remain an unrelenting presence in his life.
